title: Funnel into convergence, then loop
caption: The piece funnels one worry (work disappearing) into three parallel historical case studies that converge on the same pattern — dignity from group status, not achievement — then follows a chain explaining why ordinary paid work escapes that trap, looping back at the end to the fear it opened with.

scenes.title: After Work, We'll Have Each Other

items.text: When AI ends work, relationships supply status
items.detail: If machines do all economically necessary labor, the argument goes, humans fall back on relationships for status and meaning.

items.text: Versailles ran on petty status feuds, not ideas
items.detail: Saint-Simon's memoirs show courtiers obsessed with heraldic precedence over culture or philosophy.

items.text: Etiquette curbed — not proved — ape instincts
items.detail: Elias: court ceremony was a civilizing restraint on primate dominance behavior, not its inevitable expression.

items.text: Lives built around defending class standing
items.detail: Ostrander's 1980s subjects never worked and organized life around keeping their social network 'in good order.'

items.text: Charity valued for its 'illusion of usefulness'
items.detail: Board fundraising mattered for status, not for measurable results — by the women's own admission.

items.text: Peer groups and gossip ruled over dead-end jobs
items.detail: Gans's Boston Italian-Americans spent as little time at work as possible, organizing life around close peer groups.

items.text: Amoral familism faded as options improved
items.detail: Distrust of outsiders was a rational response to poverty, and it receded as material conditions changed.

items.text: Status comes from the group, not achievement
items.detail: Across courts, old money, and peer groups, dignity depends on group membership, which makes every society of this kind clannish and exclusive.

items.text: Work gives impersonal respect, not just money
items.detail: Unlike group-based honor, work lets you earn dignity for what you do, not who you know.

items.text: Surveys and oral histories: workers want respect
items.detail: From Pew surveys to Studs Terkel's interviews, workers consistently value feeling competent and respected over enjoying the task itself.

items.text: Commercial society freed friendship from necessity
items.detail: Because relational societies struggle with equality, the market's loosening of feudal and family ties let friendship become freer.

items.text: Author's wary hope: liberal individualism survives
items.detail: The author likes her job and liberal individualism, and hopes that if a relational world is coming, it won't cost us the latter.

scenes.caption: Three historical case studies converge on one pattern, which a closing chain uses to explain — and worry about losing — what paid work actually gives us.

scenes.title: Versailles, salons, and apes

items.text: Versailles: Europe's wealthiest, most brilliant court
items.detail: Voltaire called it one of history's four great ages of light — yet its culture was dominated by status games.

items.text: Saint-Simon obsessed over heraldic precedence
items.detail: His memoirs devote hundreds of pages to disputes over emblems and ceremonial headgear, not culture or ideas.

items.text: Salons were gossip, not philosophy
items.detail: Despite their Enlightenment reputation, salon attendees mostly talked politics and each other, not ideas.

items.text: Lilti: salon talk was mostly political gossip
Catherine's Petersburg: same gossip-driven pattern
items.detail: Even a brilliant, pragmatic ruler's court ran on tracking who offended whom to gain favor.

items.text: Aristocratic dignity: honor, not diligence
items.detail: Bourgeois dignity comes from being productive; aristocratic dignity comes from maintaining rank and family distinction.

items.text: Aristocrats act like status-obsessed chimpanzees
items.detail: Constant tracking of alliances, challenges, and displays of rank resembles primate dominance hierarchies.

items.text: Elias: civilizing, not fixed, instinct
items.detail: Versailles behavior reflected centuries of specific feudal institutions, not an inevitable return to primate nature.

scenes.caption: A chain of escalating evidence that aristocratic life without work was petty and status-obsessed, ending with a caveat that this need not be our fate.

scenes.title: Why work gives respect

items.text: Work supplies impersonal respect and competence
items.detail: The central claim: paid work's main gift, besides money, is a way to earn dignity for what you do rather than who you know.

items.text: 85% of workers report job satisfaction
items.detail: Pew, Gallup, and The Conference Board surveys agree, even for unglamorous jobs.

items.text: Strauss: COVID return showed pride, relief
items.detail: Workers returning from lockdown spoke of feeling useful again, not of loving their tasks.

items.text: FWP interviews: work mattered as much as family
items.detail: Depression-era life stories rated pride in work and recognition by peers alongside family and community.

items.text: Terkel's Working: respect beat job content
items.detail: 1970s Chicago workers hated disrespect far more than repetition, and prized being useful to peers.

items.text: Relational societies struggle with moral equality
items.detail: When dignity depends on group membership, societies get clannish — policing who belongs and who doesn't.

items.text: Commercial society freed friendship from necessity
items.detail: Smith, Hume, and Ferguson argued that once labor meets our needs, friendship can rest on sympathy rather than transaction.

items.text: Author's wary hope: liberal individualism survives
items.detail: If a more relational future is coming, the author hopes we keep the freedom commercial society gave our relationships.

scenes.caption: Four kinds of evidence feed one claim about what work supplies, which then explains why commercial society freed friendship — and the author's wary conclusion.
